en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
Sahadhammika-vagga 77.
The Training Rule on Intentional Action.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the group of six monks intentionally instilled remorse in the group of seventeen monks, saying:
"Friends, a training rule has been laid down by the Blessed One:
'A person less than twenty years of age is not to be ordained.'"
"You have been ordained with less than twenty years [of seniority].
Are you not, in fact, unordained? They wept.
The bhikkhus said,
“Friends, why are you weeping?
“Friends, these bhikkhus of the group of six are intentionally instilling remorse in us.”
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires … [as above] … complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
“How can the group-of-six bhikkhus intentionally cause remorse in bhikkhus? … [The Buddha asked:
“Is it true, bhikkhus, that you intentionally cause remorse in bhikkhus?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can you, foolish men, intentionally cause remorse in the bhikkhus?”
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:

‘If any monk should intentionally cause remorse in another monk, thinking, “May he be uncomfortable for even a moment,” doing so for no other reason than that, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).’”
"But whoever" means whoever such as this... "monk" means: [as previously defined].
...pe... this is the meaning intended here by the word "bhikkhu.
"Of a bhikkhu" means of another bhikkhu.
"Intentionally" means:
knowing, perceiving, and having deliberately willed it, there is a transgression.
"He would give rise to remorse" means:

“If you think, ‘I believe you have been ordained for less than twenty years,’ ‘I believe you have eaten at the wrong time,’ ‘I believe you have drunk liquor,’ or ‘I believe you have sat in private with a woman’— if one causes such remorse to arise, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
‘Making this very condition, and no other’ means that there is no other circumstance whatsoever for causing such remorse to arise.”
If one intentionally causes remorse in one who is ordained, perceiving that person as ordained, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one intentionally causes remorse in one who is ordained, being uncertain of their status, there is an offense of expiation.
If one intentionally causes remorse in one who is ordained, perceiving that person as not ordained, there is an offense of expiation.
If one intentionally causes remorse in one who is not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one perceives as fully ordained one who is not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one is in doubt regarding one who is not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If [the person] is not ordained and one perceives them as not ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
There is no offense if one does not intend to cause anxiety, thinking: "I think you were ordained when you were under twenty years of age; I think you [were ordained] at an improper time."
If one says, "I think you have eaten [meat], I think you have drunk liquor, I think you have sat in private with a woman;
come now, find out [the truth], lest you have remorse later," this refers to one who is insane.
"For one who is a first-time offender.
The seventh training rule concerning intentional action is finished.
